en: Preface to the Commentary on the Heart Sūtra:
When the Buddhas and Patriarchs came from the West, they did not establish written words. Why, then, do the scriptures of *bānzhòu* (chanting) number as many as five thousand?
It is because they feared that those who rely upon vines and creepers would, by indulging in verbal explanations, fall into entanglements and obscure their own nature.
The core [of his teaching] was that while the five thousand *bānfan* (chanting texts) extensively expound the nature-school (*xìngzōng*), they sever all entanglements;
though these chants are numerous, their ultimate aim does not lie beyond this single collection, the *Heart Sūtra*. Indeed, the *Heart Sūtra* is the source that unifies and synthesizes all sūtras.
The statement that it is "neither arising nor ceasing" refers to the nature of the past and future, which is fundamentally ever-present.

The statement that it is "neither defiled nor pure" refers to the nature of the deluded and the sagely, which is inherently awakened. The statement that it is "neither increasing nor decreasing" refers to the nature of longevity and brevity, and of fortune and its limit.
This is the fundamental suchness (*tathatā*). Alas, those wriggling creatures do not understand the original intent from time immemorial;

they give rise to deluded thoughts of birth and extinction, defilement and purity, increase and decrease. Consequently, the five aggregates and six consciousnesses are inverted therein; the entanglements are already extreme and the knots are already severe.
To seek to realize *prajñā* under such conditions is like driving north while heading south—just as [the story of] Sheshu Ruo and Zhongzi Hui.

The five thousand verses of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* encompass the entire essence of the scriptures; thus, commentaries (*zhù*) and sub-commentaries (*shū*) were composed. The commentary explains the tangled vines, while the sub-commentary unties the knots.
If one examines this compilation, it constitutes the essential core of the more than five thousand scrolls—the secret treasury that does not rely on words and letters.
Thus, one knows that the *Heart Sūtra* is the ultimate destination of all sūtras, and that these commentaries and sub-commentaries, in turn...
This is the essential purport of the Heart Sūtra. Those endowed with the illumination of wisdom will discern this clearly.

In the winter of the fourteenth year of the Kangxi era, during the latter part of the middle month, the monk [name] joins his palms in reverence and provides this commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
Compiled with annotations by Zhong Zhi-ping Shu-ruo-fu of Qing Ji-xing;
edited and published by Shen Hong Jian-si-fu of Xiushui.

The *Shenseng zhuan* (Biographies of Divine Monks) records that during the Zhenguan era, the Tang monk Xuanzang was dispatched on an official mission to Western India to retrieve various [scriptures].
Carrying the scriptures and images, he arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra. As he approached, the path was perilous and difficult;

there he saw an elderly monk whose head and face were covered in sores and wounds, sitting alone upon his bed in profound stillness. Xuanzang, perceiving that the monk possessed the Way, prostrated himself before him in worship.
He hoped for some instruction. The monk orally transmitted one fascicle of the *Heart Sūtra* and commanded him to recite it.
Thereupon, the mountains and rivers became level and easy to traverse, and tigers and leopards vanished from sight. It is said that *mahā* is a designation for the ultimate great;

the essence of the mind is vast and empty, such that it cannot be constrained by the four directions or the zenith and nadir. *Prajñā* is the wisdom of the mind. *Pāra* means "the other shore," which is *nirvāṇa*.
"Pan" (槃) signifies that its magnitude and minuteness are all-encompassing, with its warp and woof clearly distinguished. "Mi" (蜜) signifies the inclusion of the myriad dharmas;
it is like honey that ferments the Great Harmony (*taihe*) and stores the myriad flowers.

Before the honey is formed, the flavor of the flowers differs—distinguished by saltiness, bitterness, acidity, and pungency—and their colors differ, varying between blue, yellow, red, and white. Once the honey is perfected, all [these distinctions]...

Tastes merge into a single flavor; all forms transform into a single form. The Bodhisattva, through the nature of Prajñā, subdues body and mind and transforms various habitual tendencies so that they return to a single perfect penetration (*ekābhisamaya*). Their serenity and contentment are without distinction.
Because Prajñā is the great *dhāraṇī* (total retention) of the six *pāramitās*, it is called "many. "Many" means numerous. One interpretation says: *Pāra-*... [text ends]
The three characters "mi" (蜜) are connected [to form "paramita"]. In the West, there is a tree named *pāramitā*; its fruit is sweet and delicious, and eating it can eliminate all suffering.
"All" (*yi-qie*) has the meaning of "many. "Prajñā" is the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment;
therefore, it is directly pointed out as the "mind. "Jing" (經) means "constant. This is the constant mind shared by both the holy and the ordinary; thus, it is called *prajñā*.
In the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*,

from the passage "When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*" up to "suffering and distress," this is the narrative concerning the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara as recorded at the time Ānanda compiled the Dharma-piṭaka.
The meritorious practice of saving sentient beings constitutes the specific introduction (*prastāvanā*). The first phrase is the general prologue for the entire treatise.

The phrase "practice of the profound" (*gambhīra-pratipatti*) explains the cause, which is the internal contemplation (*adhyātma-vipaśyanā*) that is cultivated. The phrase "perceiving clearly" (*vipaśyati*) explains the fruit, which is the attainment of mastery.

The phrase "saving all" (*sarvasattvān parimocayati*) explains the bodhisattva stage that is realized. These three phrases concerning the "practice of the profound" constitute the general prologue for the entire treatise.
In summary: "Contemplation" refers to awakening. In its intrinsic state, it is quiescent illumination that is spontaneous;
in its manifestation, it is suchness, unmoving. To awaken and attain mastery is to become a Bodhisattva. Such autonomous Bodhisattvas exist in every person.

It is only because they are obstructed by the six sense faculties that they are unable to contemplate and examine themselves; being dragged by myriad passions, they fail to attain autonomy. If one is a person of wisdom... [one partakes of this].
With a pure mind, one calmly contemplates the fundamental nature and realizes that one is a Bodhisattva who has severed all ties to dharmas;
thus, one dwells in sovereign ease. Therefore, Avalokiteśvara is a Bodhisattva capable of cultivating Prajñā.
Prajñāpāramitā is the dharma cultivated by Bodhisattvas. By means of Prajñā, the Bodhisattva employs the illumination of wisdom to contemplate.
It is fully realized and perfectly interfused without obstruction; therefore, it is called "sovereign mastery. This is the practice for one's own benefit.

Furthermore, out of compassion for sentient beings mired in delusion, he causes them to cultivate this Dharma so that they may reform evil and transform toward good, leaving suffering behind and attaining happiness, achieving sovereignty in all things.
This is the practice for the benefit of others. "Bodhisattva" is a Sanskrit term for *bodhisattva*; in this language, it means "one who awakens sentient beings."

The term "Bodhisattva" alone is used here as an abbreviation. "Practice" (*xing*) means cultivation. "Profound" (*shen*) means subtle, deep, and far-reaching, such that it cannot be fathomed or discerned.
"Profound Prajñā" refers to the Prajñā of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Among the various practices of a Bodhisattva, there are none that are not *pāramitās*;
they integrate all myriad virtues and reach the ultimate stage—a realm that is not for those of coarse minds or shallow wisdom.
When one contemplates, it is the moment of seeing the original nature; this is what the ancients called "forgetting while suddenly remembering" or "suddenly waking from a dream.
One clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby transcending all suffering and distress.
The ultimate state of void lucidity is naturally such that not even a hair’s breadth is obscured; it pierces through all manner of ignorance. Hence it is said:
"To perceive that the five aggregates (*skandhas*) are all empty. "Perceive" (*zhào*) means to contemplate. "Aggregates" (*yùn*) refers to that which is accumulated and congealed.
The "five" are, as stated below, form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. These five accumulate and do not disperse, and are thus able to obscure the true nature. Only...

The Bodhisattva is able to perceive clearly at all times. While complying with the causal conditions of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) to undergo coming and going, not even a hair’s breadth of affliction can invade or disturb them;

therefore, it is said that "all are empty. All sufferings arise in dependence upon the aggregates; since the five aggregates no longer exist, one transcends the cycle of birth and death and attains liberation from all things.
Therefore, it is said that "one crosses over all suffering and calamity. To "cross over" means to be liberated.
"Deliverance" (tuō) means liberation. "All" (yīqiè) refers to the multitude. "Calamity" (è) denotes obstruction and the failure of free passage.
To be able to cross over such suffering and calamity is the wondrous function of profound practice.
Śāriputra, Śāriputra—this disciple of the Buddha is foremost in wisdom. The Buddha called him by name and addressed him: "Śā" refers to a house;
it is a metaphor for the physical body composed of the four great elements and the five aggregates. "Putra" means the original master within that house.
This is what is meant by "manifesting the physical form.

Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. This is also true for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

It is also thus. This clarifies that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally empty; it is for this reason that the meaning of "profound practice" is detailed, in accordance with the intent of the character *guan* (contemplation).
Whatever has form is called "form" (*rūpa*), which refers to the forms of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Among these six faculties, human beings are most easily attached.
Regarding "characteristics": form (*rūpa*) is the most prominent. Therefore, I single out the word "form" and repeat it again and again.
That which has no shape is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). Do not think that when I speak of emptiness, you should seek emptiness outside of form; in reality, form is not different from emptiness.
This phrase overturns the inverted views of ordinary beings, stating that the mind must not be attached to form (*rūpa*).
The phrase "emptiness is not different from form" awakens the biased views of those of the Two Vehicles, teaching that one must likewise not be attached to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

However, because it is difficult to comprehend how they are not different, the view of form and emptiness as distinct entities still persists. To explain this accordingly: "form is not different from emptiness" means that form is itself...

This is emptiness. That "emptiness is not different from form" means that emptiness is itself form. Knowing that form and emptiness are not different, one does not cling to form, nor does one cling to emptiness.
As it is with the single aggregate of form, so too for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one does not cling to them, just as one does not cling to the emptiness of form.
What the mind experiences is called feeling (*vedanā*); what it conceptualizes is called perception (*saṃjñā*); and what it constructs is called mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
Discrimination is called consciousness; this is the essential point of this sutra, the heart of Prajñā.
Śāriputra, the mark of the emptiness of all dharmas is that they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
This Bodhisattva further addressed Śāriputra: "These dharmas" refers to the aforementioned five aggregates (*skandhas*).

This clarifies that true emptiness is fundamentally without aggregates. Emptiness is originally not a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); however, because we are now discussing all dharmas, one may also use the emptiness of these dharmas to elucidate characteristics.
Therefore, it is said that "emptiness gives rise to [characteristics]"; this is the characteristic of the non-characteristic.

Thus, this is not an emptiness of annihilation, but rather the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of ultimate emptiness. Within this true reality of ultimate emptiness, wondrous awakening is eternally pervasive;
it is suchness (*tathatā*), immovable. What arising and ceasing could there be? Untainted by even a single speck of dust, if one seeks its characteristic of purity, it cannot be found;
how much less so its defilement! This is the absence of both stain and purity; the Sage has nothing further to add.
The deluded have nothing to lose; what increase or decrease could there be? The essence of the true mark of ultimate emptiness is originally just like this.

If one seeks emptiness apart from form, then that which does not arise would immediately cease, that which does not cease would immediately arise, that which is not defiled would be pure, that which is not pure would be defiled, that which does not increase would decrease, and that which does not decrease would increase. How could such a thing be spoken of as the true mark of ultimate emptiness?
Consider this: if that which is visible can be made empty, then sentient beings are themselves bodhisattvas; if it cannot be made empty, then bodhisattvas are themselves sentient beings.
Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
This leads to non-attainment. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the Great Vehicle, one should realize that these aggregates are all empty phenomena, thereby returning to the true essence.

This is because it is explained in detail that the originally empty truth has never had aggregates, in accordance with the sovereign intent [of the teaching]. "Non-existence" (*wu*) is precisely emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Therefore, the four characters "emptiness" and "non-existence" run through to the phrase "also non-attainment. As soon as one speaks of "form" (*rūpa*), [it is already subsumed within this framework].
There is no form within emptiness. Yet worldly people seek form within emptiness, not realizing that there is no form within emptiness.
Only when all things are completely swept away is the true mark of true emptiness revealed; this is the supernatural power of Prajñā.
Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. The five aggregates are empty.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomenon.
When these congeal, they become the six sense organs, and thus there are the eye, ear, and so forth. When these float, they become the six sense objects, and thus there are form, sound, and so forth.
Yet, upon investigation, it is found that the eye unites with form, the ear with sound, the nose with odor, and the tongue with taste.
"Union. The body unites with tangibles; the mind unites with mental objects (*dharma*). "Tangibles" refers to sensory contact; "mental objects" refers to the deliberative mind.
Without eyes, ears, and so forth, the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are empty. Without forms, sounds, and so forth, the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are empty.
This is the emptiness of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). As for "bases," it means that the six sense objects and the six consciousnesses mutually interpenetrate.
There is no eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), and so forth, up to no consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*).
"Element" (*dhātu*) refers to the sphere of objects. That which perceives is the eye-element; that which discriminates between right and wrong is the consciousness-element.
"Non-elemental" (amudhātu) refers to that which does not arise in the mind. Since the twelve bases (āyatana) do not exist, the eighteen elements (dhātu) likewise do not exist;
thus, the eighteen elements are empty. The eighteen elements consist of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses.
"And so forth" means that from this point one ascends to heaven and proceeds to the Land of Ultimate Bliss; the merit thereby created is immeasurable.
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; even unto old age and death, there is none, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.

The essence of its nature is serene and still, yet because of a single moment of deluded movement, one is deluded regarding the fundamental nature and thus becomes ignorant and lacks clear understanding.
Entering the vehicle of the Bodhisattva, one thereby advances to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha, not being attached to or harboring thoughts of greed, anger, or delusion.
There is no ignorance; moreover, together with the thought of ignorance, it is entirely non-existent. This continues until there is no suffering of birth and death;
the true nature is not worn away for ten thousand kalpas and is free from aging and death. Moreover, together with the thought of aging and death, it is entirely non-existent.
Thus, the twelve links of dependent origination are empty. The phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) indicates that the beginning and end have been cited while the middle has been abbreviated.
Within this, although their fundamental nature is empty, the stages between them are not one and the same. The twelve links of dependent origination and the five aggregates share the same meaning;
however, when summarized they are five, and when detailed they are twelve, encompassing the causes and effects of the three periods of time.
They depend upon one another in succession, revolving like a wheel without rest.
There is no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path;
having transcended birth and death, even the physical form is forgotten. Yet there is still suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path. "Suffering" refers to birth and old age.

The "fruits" refer to the various sufferings of birth, illness, and death. The "accumulation" refers to the gathering of afflictions, karma, and the causes of all suffering—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion;
these are mundane phenomena. "Cessation" refers to the complete extinction of the sufferings of birth and death arising from desire; this is the blissful fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
The Way refers to morality, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; these are the causes of happiness. Second, there are supramundane dharmas.
By means of these, one advances in the Śrāvaka vehicle, yet without [conceptually] cognizing suffering or severing its origin, one aspires for cessation and cultivates the path.
By emptying all afflictions, one attains great sovereignty; thus, the Four Noble Truths are empty.
There is neither ignorance nor attainment;
by this one enters the Bodhisattva vehicle. Since there are no five aggregates (*skandha*), four truths (*satya*), or any dharmas, it may be called wisdom.
Yet, because emptiness causes one to forget all that exists, one does not even perceive it as wisdom—this is "non-ignorance. Upon reaching this state...

One traverses the path and attains realization within the realm of phenomena; yet emptiness remains the original substance, never adding anything to that which was originally non-existent. Thus, what could be seen as "attainment"?
Because there is nothing to be attained, true emptiness is signless;
person and phenomena are both forgotten, and both the truths and emptiness are discarded. If one seeks the reason for this, one likewise cannot know why it is so.
Why? Because self-nature is fundamentally without substance; this is because there is nothing to be attained. This concludes the [section].
The preceding section on emptiness and signlessness concludes; this now begins the passage concerning the subsequent attainment of the fruit by Bodhisattvas and Buddhas.
A Bodhisattva, by virtue of relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has no hindrance in the mind. Because there is no hindrance in the mind...
There is no fear; one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, reaching ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
This, along with the following section, explains in detail how one transcends all suffering and calamity. By contemplating emptiness through wisdom, one reaches the other shore.
The practice of a Bodhisattva does not consist merely of emptying existence, but also emptying non-existence; it does not merely empty the false, but furthermore...
Emptiness is the truth; this is the profundity of true practice, and it constitutes the Bodhisattva. "Bodhi" means awakening; "sattva" means a sentient being.
While all living beings are sentient beings, only the Bodhisattva among sentient beings has attained awakening;
therefore, they are called "Awakened Sentient Beings. Sattva is the person who is the locus of reliance. Prajñāpāramitā...
*Prajñāpāramitā*. This is the Dharma upon which one relies. By relying on this gateway of Prajñā, the Bodhisattva practices and studies;

when their merit is perfected and their principle is fulfilled, the nature of awakening becomes all-pervasive and unobstructed, *pāramitā* becomes vast and expansive, true emptiness is profound and still, and the myriad objects of experience are as they are.

This is stated by pushing the analysis to its ultimate limit. To have uninterrupted discursive thought is called "entanglement" (*guà*); to be attached to objects is... [the remainder of the sentence is missing from the source].
That which does not turn back is called an obstruction. For a Bodhisattva, both the internal and external are pure; all conditions are liberated, and the mind is free from the bonds of karma.
What further obstructions could there be? When ordinary people experience anxiety, fear, and terror, it is always because they cling to something.
Once these obstructions have been removed, then birth and death are equalized, evil conditions are silenced, and how could there be any further fear or dread?

It is indeed fearful. Dreams arise from conceptualization, and conceptualization arises from recollection. When a Bodhisattva forgets emotional attachments and severs craving, forever cutting off the delusions and awakenings of inverted views and the dream-like fantasies of false memory, the causes of suffering are exhausted.
Reaching the ultimate state of tranquility, they eternally delight in the fruit of Buddhahood—neither arising nor ceasing. Is this not the state of Great Sovereignty? As it is said:
Thus does one transcend all suffering and calamity.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This Dharma of the pāramitās is not only practiced and realized by bodhisattvas; all Buddhas likewise follow it together.
The aforementioned ultimate nirvāṇa is precisely the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna); the Buddha-nature is non-dual.
Therefore, there have been no Buddhas of the three periods— past, present, and future— who did not rely upon this Prajñā-dharma to cultivate sublime practices,
thereby penetrating the purity of their own nature, realizing true emptiness, and attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When the term "Nirvāṇa" is used for Bodhisattvas and "Bodhi" is used for Buddhas, it is merely a matter of alternating the phrasing to reveal the underlying meaning.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra,
an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra.
"Dhāraṇī" means a mantra; it also signifies a prayer or aspiration. It refers to the fulfillment of all that one seeks according to one's vows.

Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of sentient beings are deep and heavy, they cannot be eliminated instantaneously; therefore, the Buddha provisionally employs the power of mantras to enable them to attain liberation.

Indeed, whether it be a Bodhisattva’s realization of *nirvāṇa* or a Buddha’s attainment of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), neither occurs apart from the cultivation of *prajñā* (wisdom). Thus...
To know this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā is to be able to destroy demonic obstacles;
it is the Great Divine Mantra, that is, the incantation of unfathomable transformations. This refers back to the emptiness of the five aggregates, which can extinguish the darkness of ignorance.
This is the Great Illuminating Mantra; it refers to the *dhāraṇī* that illuminates and realizes all delusions.
"Great" means it cannot be compared to the small powers or small wisdom of others. It can manifest the ultimate principle, the most supreme *Ekayāna*, to which nothing further can be added;
thus it is called the Unsurpassed Mantra. It is the fruit of the most wondrous awakening, peerless and without equal.
"Lun. This is called the "Spell of the Peerless" (*asamasama*). It refers to the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*), signifying that he is supreme.
By repeating "unsurpassed and equal," it expresses the profound attachment to Prajñā, which is vast and boundless. Only true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is sufficient to embody this.
It can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.

The efficacy of this *prajñā* bond is vast and great. By practicing in reliance upon it, one will forever awaken without delusion, and be able to sever all afflictions, birth and death, as well as inverted thoughts, dreams, and the like. This is truly and not falsely so.
"Disciples, you should receive and practice these words.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is spoken. It is spoken as follows: [mantra].
Thus, when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak this Prajñāpāramitā, it is the secret language of the Buddhas; it is not..."

This is what ordinary people know. To recite the incantation and pray that others may be like oneself—when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak an incantation, they wish that all sentient beings may, just as they have, attain perfect enlightenment. The incantation refers to the final four lines of the verse.
If one can recite this incantation, then whatever one wishes for will be accomplished without fail. Let us explain this by means of a *mantra*.
*Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*. This mantra summarizes the preceding text. *Gata* means "to reveal" or "to manifest.
*Gati* means "aggregation" or "meaning. *Pāra* means "the other shore. *Saṃ* signifies the purity of body and mind.
*Bodhi* refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. *Svāhā* is [equivalent to] *mā*... [end of fragment].
"Hā" is a term of supreme praise; it signifies that the purport of the entire scripture is none other than the clear revelation of the bodhisattva’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
As for why this reveals the ultimate truth: it is because it clearly demonstrates the Buddha-truth for the sake of reaching the other shore (*pāra*).
Yet, even this is not something to be obstructed by names and signs (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), for it is for the purpose of arriving there.
He reveals the Truth upon the ground of ultimate purity on the shore; by means of this, he realizes the fruit of Buddhahood and attains Bodhi.
Since this is the supreme realm of a Bodhisattva, how could it possibly be limited?
Commentary on the Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom (Concluded)
